nameStory: This honeysuckle earned its 'swamp' name from its love of wet, boggy places where many other honeysuckles fear to tread. The 'fly honeysuckle' part comes from its paired flowers that dangle like little flying insects from the branches. Its scientific name 'oblongifolia' simply means 'oblong leaves,' describing the elongated oval shape of its foliage.
description: Swamp fly honeysuckle is a native deciduous shrub that grows 3-6 feet tall in New England's wetlands. It has a somewhat open, irregular branching pattern that gives it a wild, untamed appearance. The plant produces small, pale yellow tubular flowers in pairs during late spring, followed by red berries in summer. Unlike many of its more aggressive honeysuckle cousins, this native species is well-behaved and beneficial to local wildlife.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Paired pale yellow or greenish-white tubular flowers hang from short stalks, about half an inch long with a sweet, delicate fragrance that's much subtler than Japanese honeysuckle

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oblong leaves arranged in opposite pairs, 2-4 inches long with smooth edges and a soft, slightly fuzzy texture on the underside

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Bright red berries appear in pairs but often fuse together at the base, creating a distinctive heart-shaped or double-berry appearance

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Open, somewhat scraggly shrub with thin, reddish-brown stems that feel smooth when young but develop a slightly shredding bark texture with age

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Found exclusively in wet areas like swamps, bogs, and stream edges where the soil stays consistently moist or soggy underfoot

habitat: Look for swamp fly honeysuckle in New England's wetlands, particularly acidic bogs, swampy areas, and along stream banks where the soil stays consistently moist. It thrives in areas too wet for most other shrubs, often growing alongside winterberry, swamp azalea, and various sedges. You'll rarely find it in upland areas or well-drained soils.

seasonality.spring: Pale yellow paired flowers appear in late May to early June, dangling gracefully from the branches with a subtle sweet scent. New leaves emerge with a fresh green color and soft texture.
seasonality.summer: Bright red berries develop in July and August, often appearing fused in pairs. The foliage remains green and provides good identification through leaf shape and arrangement.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow-green to brown before dropping. Berries may persist into early fall, providing food for birds before eventually being consumed or dropping.
seasonality.winter: Bare reddish-brown stems with smooth bark show the opposite branching pattern. Small buds are visible, and the wet habitat location becomes a key identification clue.

funFact: With only 12 recorded observations in all of New England, finding a swamp fly honeysuckle is like discovering botanical treasure—you're more likely to spot a moose than this elusive native shrub!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other fly honeysuckles, but the consistently wet habitat is your best clue—if your feet aren't getting soggy, you're probably looking at American fly honeysuckle or mountain fly honeysuckle instead. The paired, often-fused red berries also help distinguish it from the separate berries of its relatives.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the honeysuckle name fool you into thinking this is an invasive pest like Japanese honeysuckle. This native species is actually quite rare and ecologically valuable, supporting native pollinators and birds without the aggressive spreading behavior of its non-native relatives.
compareHints: Unlike the more common American fly honeysuckle which prefers drier woods, swamp fly honeysuckle demands wet feet and boggy conditions. Its berries often fuse together in pairs more consistently than other fly honeysuckles. The mountain fly honeysuckle has hairier leaves and grows at higher elevations in rockier soils, making habitat your best distinguishing feature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the invasive Japanese, Morrow's, and Tatarian honeysuckles that dominate many New England areas, American fly-honeysuckle has distinctively paired berries and a much more restrained growth habit.
Japanese honeysuckle is unique among New England honeysuckles for its white-to-yellow color change and semi-evergreen leaves.
Unlike native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Morrow's honeysuckle has flowers and berries strictly in pairs with red fruit.
Unlike native American fly-honeysuckle which stays small and has paired flowers on long stalks, Amur honeysuckle grows into a large shrub with flowers sitting directly on the branches.
Among New England honeysuckles, coral honeysuckle is the only one with scentless, coral-red tubular flowers and that distinctive leaf-fusion around the stem.
Among New England's honeysuckles, glaucous honeysuckle is the only climbing species with that distinctive waxy blue-green leaf coating and cup-forming fused upper leaves.
Unlike our native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Tatarian honeysuckle always has paired flowers and red berries.
Mountain fly-honeysuckle differs from American fly honeysuckle by having much fuzzier leaves and preferring higher elevation habitats.
Among New England's honeysuckles, the dense coating of soft hairs immediately separates this species from smooth-leaved Japanese honeysuckle or the only slightly hairy American fly honeysuckle.
Fly honeysuckle stands out from other honeysuckles in New England by its paired red berries and shrubby growth habit - most others either climb like vines or have different colored berries.
Unlike the vigorous vining Japanese honeysuckle, winter honeysuckle is a well-behaved shrub that doesn't climb.

Unlike the ubiquitous Japanese honeysuckle which blooms white to yellow and has simple opposite leaves, common honeysuckle has those distinctive fused upper leaves and more intensely fragrant flowers.
While New England has many honeysuckle species, perfoliate honeysuckle is the only one with fused upper leaves that the stem appears to grow through.
Unlike the invasive Asian honeysuckles that plague New England (Japanese, Morrow's, Amur), twinberry honeysuckle doesn't spread aggressively and has the unique twin-berry-in-red-bracts feature.
Unlike the aggressive Japanese honeysuckle that stays white then turns yellow, grape honeysuckle flowers age to pink.
Unlike its weedy relatives like Japanese honeysuckle (which climbs) or Morrow's honeysuckle (which has red berries), sweetberry honeysuckle stays compact and produces edible blue fruit.
